newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Major trading partners blast U.S. unilateralism.
newsitem.headline: Major trading partners blast U.S. unilateralism.

text.p: Major trading nations, including Japan and the European Union, expressed concern Tuesday over the United States resorting to unilateral, punitive trade measures, senior trade diplomats said.

Textile-exporting countries in Asia and Latin America also criticised Washington for slow implementation of a global accord to phase out restrictions on textile and clothing imports over a 10-year period, they added.

Deputy Trade Representative Jeffrey Lang defended U.S. laws at the two-day meeting at the World Trade Organisation, which heard calls for U.S. leadership to wrap up negotiations on financial services, telecommunications and maritime transport.

Lang said that use of Section 301 of the U.S. trade law, which launches investigations into allegedly unfair foreign practices, was a means for communicating exporters' concerns. It was integrally linked to bringing disputes to the WTO forum.
However, Lang declined to comment on extra-territorial application of U.S. legislation including the Helms-Burton Act.
The debate, attended by most of WTO's 125 member states, centred on a study by WTO economists of the U.S. trade regime.
The lengthy report said that the United States, the world's largest trading nation, must keep its markets open and resist pressures at home to take unilateral trade measures.
A liberal and predictable U.S. market would help maintain growth in domestic productivity and was also vital for the health of the international trading system, the trade watchdog said.

But Washington had continued with regional, bilateral and unilateral trade initiatives, and its multi-track approach including investigations under Section 301 could be a source of tension within the multilateral system, according to the report.

Member states welcomed U.S. tariff-cutting commitments under the 1994 Uruguay Round trade accord and the low average of U.S. tariffs, according to Anne Anderson, the Irish ambassador who chairs WTO's trade policy review body.
Recent U.S. reforms in agriculture and telecommunications, and a drop in the use of anti-dumping measures were commended.

"Contradictory signals were noted. Despite the stated commitment to multilateralism and frequent invocation of WTO dispute settlement procedures, we still have some evidence of a resort to unilateral approaches," she told a final news briefing after the closed-door talks ended in Geneva.
"A general dissatisfaction with the continued unilateralism inherent in 'Section 301' legislation was expressed.

"A number of delegations expressed their objections to the unilateral use of trade policy instruments for non-trade policy objectives. In this context, the Helms-Burton Act and the Iran-Libya Trade Sanctions Act were particularly mentioned and the WTO consistency of these measures was strongly questioned."
"Section 301 was raised by a very good cross-section of countries, including Japan, Canada, the EU, South Korea, Colombia and Chile," Anderson said. "There was a chorus."
She added: "Criticisms of legislative provisions with extra-territorial effect were widely shared."

The EU is on course to win establishment of a WTO dispute settlement panel on Nov. 20 to examine its complaint that the Helms-Burton law punishing foreign companies in Cuba violates WTO free trade laws.

On textiles, some members expressed disappointment that the U.S. integration of textile and clothing products under the four-phase agreement was heavily backloaded. These included Colombia, Thailand, India, Pakistan and Hong Kong.
"It was considered that this violated the spirit of a gradual phasing-in of the products covered by the WTO agreement and could inhibit the adjustment process in the U.S. market," Anderson said.

Lang responded that the U.S. textile market -- the world's largest -- was a sensitive sector employing many vulnerable Americans but had high import penetration. Going beyond announced plans was not out of the question but would depend on other countries's willingness to undertake commensurate moves.

WTO's report said: "While an open, predictable world trading system continues to be crucial for the well-being of the U.S. economy, the converse is also true; an open, predictable U.S. economy is crucial for the health of the world trading system.

"It is therefore crucial that the United States and its partners utilize the system to maintain multilateralism as the key to future developments and discourage pressures for increased bilateralism or unilateralism," it added.
